output.methodChoice: Evidence-ledger provenance check, then Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (Kepner-Tregoe-style IS/IS NOT on installer and firmware splits)
output.brief: The VA-220 failures trace to Pellacott's 2026-built valves, not to the new installers or firmware 4.2. The quality-lab data matched to serial numbers shows the same claim rate (about 41–42 per 1,000) for legacy and new installers and for firmware 4.1 and 4.2. Durrant-Hale valves stay at 5–7 per 1,000 in every group. Never-installed Pellacott 2026 valves leak at the seat 11% of the time, against 1% for 2025 builds and 0% for Durrant-Hale. The calibration contractor found Pellacott's leak-test rig out of service since January 2026, with no VA-220 test program on any other rig. Certificate values repeat four fixed sequences, which also appear in November 2025 certificates. So the certificates very likely do not reflect real tests. That also explains the score rise, since the score rewarded complete certificates. Do not release the six held lots on fresh certificates, and do not penalise the installers. Quarantine 2026-built Pellacott stock, suspend dock-to-stock, and run your own helium leak testing before release. Plan for line impact by sourcing more from Durrant-Hale. Check whether other suppliers' records are genuine, and tie scoring to rig logs. The seal change is a plausible mechanism but isn't separable from the line move. Confidence is high.
